text._main: Regional anaesthesia · Lower limb Lower-limb blocks Blocks for the hip, knee, thigh, ankle and foot: how to do them, what they cover and what they weaken, and which one to choose for the operation in front of you. Created by Dr Koh Wenjun and Dr Chew Shi Hao, NTF Anaesthesia For education only. Follow local guidelines and senior advice; check doses for each patient. Four pages Choose a region Each page covers anatomy, position, equipment, technique, dose, coverage and complications, with animated demonstrations, a simulated ultrasound scan with the needle and spread, exam questions, and consultant and frontier notes. Page 1 · Hip Hip PENG and lateral femoral cutaneous Fascia iliaca, supra- and infra-inguinal Femoral nerve block The hip fracture pathway Open the hip page → Page 2 · Knee Knee Femoral triangle and adductor canal iPACK and genicular nerve blocks Obturator, and the obturator jerk The motor-sparing knee plan Open the knee page → Page 3 · Foot and ankle Foot and ankle Popliteal sciatic Ankle block, ultrasound and landmark Saphenous at and below the knee Tourniquets, foot drop, the numb heel Open the foot and ankle page → Page 4 · Thigh Thigh and amputation Subgluteal sciatic, and the other levels Posterior femoral cutaneous nerve Amputation planner Block combinations and total dose Open the thigh page → Rapid fire Eight things to know before any lower-limb block Femoral nerve = quadriceps. A femoral or fascia iliaca block weakens the leg: check strength before the first stand. Choose PENG or an adductor canal block when the patient must walk. Fascia iliaca does not reliably block the obturator nerve, whatever the volume. Popliteal misses the saphenous strip: the medial leg and the medial malleolus. Add a saphenous block. An ankle block numbs the foot, not the ankle joint: the joint branches leave above the malleoli. Ask where the cuff goes. Ankle cuff: ankle block. Calf cuff: popliteal + saphenous. Thigh cuff: spinal or general anaesthesia. A spinal does not stop the obturator jerk. Block the obturator nerve before the resection. A numb foot can’t warn you: float the heel, pad the fibular neck, and think compartment syndrome when new pain breaks through. Count every milligram, the surgeon’s infiltration included. A common ceiling for ropivacaine is about 3 mg/kg (lean body weight), lower in the frail. What each block costs in muscle PENGUsually none. Quadriceps weakness if fluid reaches the femoral nerve. LFCNNone. Purely sensory. Fascia iliaca, femoralQuadriceps. The knee buckles: falls. Adductor canalLargely spared. Vastus medialis if too proximal or too much volume. iPACK, genicularNone. iPACK can spread to the tibial or common peroneal nerve. ObturatorHip adductors. Sciatic, poplitealFoot drop, no push-off; the hamstrings too with the subgluteal level. AnkleIntrinsic foot muscles only. Walks on the heel.

Tibial plateau fixation or tibial nail

Achilles tendon repair
Hallux valgus or forefoot surgery
Foot debridement, toe or ray amputation

TURBT: the obturator jerk

Saphenous vein harvest or varicose vein surgery

Hip fracture: emergency department and positioning for spinal

IN ONE LINE
Fascia iliaca (or femoral) block on arrival; give or repeat a block 20–30 minutes before you sit the patient up for the spinal.

deep
deep
Lat
Med

Front

Core: must be covered
Outlined, cross-hatched shapes marked “deep”: joint or bone, not skin
The right lower limb. Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Hip joint, anterior capsule: deep: articular branches of the femoral, obturator and (when present) accessory obturator nerves
Femur: deep: femoral, sciatic and obturator branches (varies along the bone)
AREA TO COVER
The fracture and the hip joint (anterior capsule) and the femur: pain on movement, not just at rest.
Block options
RECOMMENDED
Supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block

DOSE 40 ml of 0.2% ropivacaine (80 mg), in 5 ml aliquots

Femoral nerve and LFCN by volume: the hip, the femur and the lateral thigh. Can be done after a general anaesthetic or in the emergency department by trained staff.

Supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block
(hip)
→
ALTERNATIVES
Femoral nerve block

DOSE 15 ml of 0.4% ropivacaine (60 mg)

Superficial and compressible: a sensible choice on anticoagulants. Misses the LFCN.

Femoral nerve block
(hip)
→
PENG block

DOSE 20 ml of 0.2% ropivacaine (40 mg)

Eases pain on movement with the quadriceps spared; best suited to neck of femur fractures going for arthroplasty.

PENG block
(hip)
→
Infra-inguinal fascia iliaca block

The simpler emergency department version: less cranial spread, so the LFCN is less reliably reached.

Infra-inguinal fascia iliaca
(hip)
→
What they miss
The obturator nerve: no fascia iliaca or femoral approach blocks it reliably.
The posterior capsule (sacral plexus branches): some pain on movement often remains, so check before you position.
Practical notes
Give the block 20–30 minutes before moving the patient: sitting, or lateral with the fractured side down for a unilateral spinal, becomes tolerable.
A small titrated dose of a short-acting analgesic is better than heavy sedation for positioning.
Repeat a block at surgery if at least 6 hours have passed since the first one, and count both doses towards the total.
In dementia, use an observational pain score and still block: under-treated pain adds to delirium.
Hip fracture pathway
(hip)
→
Fracture chooser
(hip)
→

Doses are ropivacaine for an adult, as used on the block pages. They are starting points: adjust for weight, age, frailty and every other local anaesthetic the patient receives.

Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity. Lower-limb combinations use large volumes, often in frail or sick patients: two or three blocks plus the surgeon’s infiltration can pass the maximum dose. Add up the milligrams before you start, inject in small aliquots with aspiration, and know where the lipid emulsion is.
